domain: Disaster Anthropology / Institutional Memory / Land-Use Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of the Aneyoshi tsunami stone's 'do not build below this line' directive, which persisted as a land-use constraint across 78 years without catastrophe validation, then proved decisive in the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami. The kernel contest centers on whether the commitment decayed to commemorative symbol or retained behavioral force during the inter-catastrophe period.

key_entities: Tsunami stone (physical marker inscribed 'High dwellings ensure peace for descendants')
Inter-catastrophe generation (residents 1933-2011 without direct tsunami experience)
key_tensions: Commemorative decay vs behavioral persistence (symbol erosion vs live constraint)
Economic pressure vs elevation constraint (coastal access value vs stone-line prohibition)

omegas.description: If 2011 tsunami had NOT occurred, would the stone directive have decayed by 2030? The 78-year gap tests commitment durability, but 2011 validation may have artificially extended what was already eroding.

Was compliance voluntary (internalized norm) or enforced (village council veto power)? Behavioral-competence reading assumes internalization; enforcement would reclassify as rope rather than mountain.
At what coastal-access economic value would the stone directive have been violated? The 78-year period may represent below-threshold conditions rather than absolute commitment.

Prompt flags D5 catastrophe-theorem break as 'decisive' but does not specify which reading it validates. If D5 validates behavioral-competence, commemorative-husk becomes empirically falsified rather than contested.

axiom_contradictions.basis: Commemorative-husk axiom (symbols decay without reinforcement) and behavioral-competence axiom (catastrophe-derived norms persist through transmission) are mutually exclusive. No framework holds both: either the directive lost force (husk) or retained it (competence), but not both simultaneously across the same 78-year period.
